info.bio: Blood, Sweat & Tears (también conocidos como BS&T) fue una banda de rock, fundada en 1967 en Nueva York (Estados Unidos), que se convirtió en el principal icono del llamado Jazz Rock, fusionando rock, blues, pop y jazz a través de arreglos complejos, concebidos para una sección rítmica clásica y una sección de instrumentos de viento, creando una peculiar forma de R&B y soul. Junto con el grupo Chicago, conforman la cabeza más visible de lo que el musicólogo Joachim E. Berendt llamó las «big bands de rock».

scenes.name: Fusión jazz-rock
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: El jazz siempre fue fusión («nada de lo que venga de Nueva Orleans es puro»), pero desde Bitches Brew (400.000 copias el primer año) la palabra significa jazz con rock, y amplía la base económica de todo el jazz en los setenta. Miles sigue con discos crudos montados por Teo Macero (Jack Johnson, Live-Evil, On the Corner) y acaba de telonero de los Headhunters de Herbie Hancock. Sus antiguos músicos fundan los grupos clave: Return to Forever de Chick Corea (sabor latino, «Spain»), la Mahavishnu Orchestra de John McLaughlin (rock a lo Hendrix, música india) y Weather Report de Zawinul y Shorter, una estética de Ellington aplicada al pop electrónico, con el bajo de Jaco Pastorius («Birdland»). Del lado del rock: Blood, Sweat & Tears, Chase, Hendrix, Sly Stone y Frank Zappa. Luego llegan el jazz pulido para la radio, Spyro Gyra y Kenny G, el M-Base de Steve Coleman y Cassandra Wilson, el acid jazz de Londres y US3, y el último Miles con el hip hop de doo-bop. Pat Metheny es el guitarrista más visionario del estilo.

podcast.title: Controversial Cold War Tour (1970)
podcast.body: In the summer of 1970, during the height of the Cold War, the band embarked on a tour of communist countries including Poland, Romania, and Yugoslavia, after the US State Department offered Canadian David Clayton Thomas permanent residency in the United States in exchange for their participation. The band was surprised by censorship and directives to play more jazz and less "rhythm" because it was deemed to be "inciting rioting." "It was the summer of 1970 and the Cold War is still hot and the band went on a tour of communist countries, Poland and Romania and Yugoslavia."

podcast.title: David Clayton Thomas' Departure (1972)
podcast.body: David Clayton Thomas left the band for three years in 1972, citing the overwhelming touring schedule as the reason. While he received songwriting royalties, most other band members relied solely on touring for their income, which perpetuated the continuous touring. "Clayton Thomas said that he left the band for three years in 1972 because the touring was too much while he was getting songwriting royalties."

podcast.title: "What the Hell Happened to Blood, Sweat & Tears" Documentary
podcast.body: A documentary, with the working title "What the Hell Happened to Blood, Sweat & Tears," was announced in November 2020. It promises to offer "humor and fresh insight" into the "strange, never-before-told story" of the band's entanglement with the Nixon administration and their controversial Iron Curtain tour, which placed them "in the crossfire of a polarized America." "It was announced in November 2020 that the documentary, at least with the working title, I don't know what it will end up with, what the hell happened to blood, sweat and tears is going to offer, I quote, humor and fresh insight into this strange, never-before-told story of a tangle with the Nixon administration, a controversial tour behind the Iron Curtain that put them in the crossfire of a polarized America."

podcast.title: Accused of Being "Sellouts"
podcast.body: Despite breaking attendance records and achieving commercial success, the band was accused of being "sellouts" by the underground rock press, a perception that intensified due to their later involvement with the US government. "All of the shows sold out and that is what blood sweat and tears were accused of being by the underground rock press sell out."

podcast.title: Accused of Being Nixon Administration Collaborators
podcast.body: Despite having protested the Vietnam War and played a concert at Kent State after the May 4th, 1970 shootings, the band was seen as "sellouts" by anti-war activists like Abby Hoffman for working on behalf of the federal government and the Nixon administration due to their Cold War tour. "They reviewed as sellouts by the likes of anti-war activists like Abby Hoffman for working on behalf of the federal government and the Nixon administration."

podcast.title: Band's Musical Identity
podcast.body: Al Kooper originally created the band with a vision of it being a rock band, but other members perceived it as a jazz band. David Clayton Thomas stated that without his R&B and soul influences, the band would have been "just a jazz band," asserting his role in making it more of a rock band. "Clayton Thomas said that without him it was just a jazz band but he brought in this R&B and this soul to make it more of a rock band."

podcast.title: First Rock Band on Vegas Strip
podcast.body: Blood, Sweat & Tears became the first rock band to play on the Las Vegas strip, performing six sold-out shows in three nights at Caesar's Palace in 1969, breaking attendance records previously held by Frank Sinatra. "it is within this environment that blood sweat and tears took to the stage at Caesar's Palace in Las Vegas for six shows in three nights in 1969. All of the shows sold out and that is what blood sweat and tears were accused of being by the underground rock press sell out."

xref.title: Early Professional Gigs and "Osterizer" (1968)
xref.body: The band's first professional gig was opening for the Amboy Dukes (featuring Ted Nugent) on January 20, 1968, followed by an opening slot for Blood Sweat and Tears on March 3, 1968. During these shows, Iggy notably played a homemade instrument called the "Osterizer," which was a vacuum cleaner attached to a blender, although he soon abandoned it due to amplification difficulties. "And was the singer playing a vacuum cleaner? Yes, yes it was. And was it attached to a blender? And yeah, it was."

xref.title: Al Cooper's Involvement (1973)
xref.body: Al Cooper of Blood Sweat and Tears was greatly impressed by the band. He signed them and facilitated their entry into a recording studio, leading to the release of their debut album, *Pronounced 'Lěh-ńérd Śkin-ńérd*, in 1973. "Al Cooper of Blood Sweat and Tears was really impressed. He signed the band and put them in the studio."
